paragraphs.heading: A war that emptied regions
paragraphs.text: The Thirty Years' War ran from 1618 to 1648 and was fought mostly in Central Europe. It ranks among the most destructive wars Europe has ever seen. Somewhere between 4.5 and 8 million soldiers and civilians died from fighting, hunger or illness. In some parts of Germany, more than half the people were gone.

paragraphs.heading: Roots in the Reformation
paragraphs.text: The trouble began with religious division inside the Holy Roman Empire, a split that grew out of the 16th-century Reformation. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 tried to settle things by sorting the empire's states into Catholic and Lutheran ones. Under a rule called cuius regio, eius religio, each state followed the faith of its ruler. That deal came under strain as Protestantism, and especially Calvinism, spread into Catholic areas after 1555. Both Lutherans and Catholics viewed Calvinism with hostility.

paragraphs.heading: A weak empire with many parts
paragraphs.text: The empire was hard to govern. It held 300 separate imperial estates spread across Germany, the Low Countries, northern Italy and France, ranging from the seven Prince-electors who chose the emperor down to bishoprics and cities like Hamburg. Its Imperial Diet, the assembly sitting over them all, met rarely and talked more than it made laws. Since 1440 the emperors had come from the House of Habsburg, the biggest landowner in the empire.

paragraphs.heading: Tension before the war
paragraphs.text: Local riots showed the strain. In 1606, at Donauwörth, the Lutheran majority blocked a Catholic procession, and Emperor Rudolf then let the Catholic Maximilian of Bavaria annex the town. When the Imperial Diet met in 1608, the Habsburg heir Ferdinand demanded that all Church property taken since 1555 be returned at once. That threat to every Protestant froze the Diet. Frederick IV of the Palatinate formed the Protestant Union in 1608, and Maximilian answered with the Catholic League in 1609.

paragraphs.heading: From local quarrel to wider war
paragraphs.text: Fighting broke out in 1618, when the Protestant Frederick V of the Palatinate replaced the Catholic Ferdinand II as king of Bohemia. Frederick was quickly removed, but the war spread into his own lands, the Palatinate. Their strategic value pulled in the Dutch Republic and Spain, while rulers such as Christian IV of Denmark and Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden saw a chance to gain imperial territory. Together with Protestant fears for their faith, this turned a quarrel between ruling families inside the empire into a far bigger conflict.

paragraphs.heading: Two phases and a peace
paragraphs.text: The war fell into two broad stages. From 1618 to 1635 it was mainly a civil war inside the empire, largely closed by the Peace of Prague. Then France joined in alliance with Sweden, and the empire became one battlefield in a larger contest against their Habsburg rivals: Emperor Ferdinand III and Spain. The Peace of Westphalia ended the fighting in 1648. It gave states like Bavaria and Saxony more freedom, handed Sweden land in northern Germany, and saw Spain accept Dutch independence.
